headword: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
sort_key: vindication of the rights of woman
entry: 1792 essay by [[Mary Wollstonecraft]], British philosopher and women's rights advocate, regarded as an early work of feminist philosophy. Written amid the [[French Revolution]], it responds to a 1791 report to the National Assembly of revolutionary France that proposed only domestic education for women. It argues that women should receive an education suited to their social role and that they deserve the same fundamental rights as men, especially in moral responsibility and educational access. Wollstonecraft intended a more thoughtful second volume but died before completing it. The essay was generally well received on publication, but her reputation suffered after William Godwin's *Memoirs of the Author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman* (1798) revealed details of her personal life. It influenced nineteenth-century women's rights advocates, including the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention. Whether Wollstonecraft supported full political rights for women is unclear.

Slender-trunked tree native to eastern Amazonia, cultivated mainly for its fruit. The species, *Euterpe oleracea*, belongs to the [[Arecaceae|palm family]]. It grows chiefly in swamps and floodplains, especially in [[Brazil]]. The fruit, or açaí berry, was a staple in floodplain areas from around the 18th century, and demand for it expanded rapidly in the 21st century. Harvesting in the rainforest employs children as young as 13, who climb trees without harnesses to collect berries, a practice that has led to falls and injuries.

American basketball player for the Las Vegas Aces of the [[Women's National Basketball Association|WNBA]]. Wilson played college basketball at the University of South Carolina, where she helped the Gamecocks win the 2017 NCAA women's championship. Drafted first overall in the 2018 WNBA draft, she has been a five-time league MVP and was the first WNBA player to win three straight MVP awards. She led the Aces to league titles in 2022, 2023 and 2025, and she has won two Olympic and two World Cup gold medals with the United States women's national team.

Two categories of knowledge, justification or argument in [[Epistemology|epistemology]], distinguished by whether they depend on sensory experience. A proposition is known or justified a priori if it can be known independently of any experience beyond what is needed to understand it. It is known a posteriori if its justification depends on empirical evidence. That it is sunny in London today is known a posteriori; that it is either sunny or not sunny there can be known a priori. Mathematics and formal logic rely predominantly on a priori justification, while most sciences involve a posteriori justification. The distinction became prominent through *Critique of Pure Reason* by [[Immanuel Kant]], who related it to the analytic–synthetic distinction. W. V. O. Quine argued that the analytic–synthetic distinction is illegitimate, challenging the analytic explanation of a priori knowledge.

Triangular massif in northern [[Niger]], within the [[Sahara]]. It rises above 1,800 m (5,900 ft) and covers 84,000 sq km (32,000 sq mi). Its plateau, at 500–900 m, has a [[Sahel]] climate, an island of vegetation amid desert that supports farming and pastoral communities. The massif is built largely of dark peralkaline [[Granite|granite]] intrusions, with volcanic features including an extinct [[Caldera|caldera]] and one of the largest ring dike systems in the world. Carboniferous sandstone and coal to the west contain [[Uranium|uranium]] derived from the massif's granites. More than 430 vascular plant species have been recorded, and seasonal rains fill stone pools called gueltas.

Graph traversal and pathfinding algorithm used in many fields of [[Computer science|computer science]]. Given a weighted graph, a source node and a goal node, it finds the shortest path between them. It can be seen as an extension of [[Dijkstra's algorithm]] that uses a [[Heuristic|heuristic]] to guide its search. Peter Hart, Nils Nilsson and Bertram Raphael first published it in 1968; it was created for the Shakey project, which aimed to build a mobile robot that could plan its own actions. Its main practical drawback is its O(bd) space complexity.

City in [[North Rhine-Westphalia]], western Germany, bordering [[Belgium]] and the Netherlands. Warm mineral springs drew Roman settlers, and the Carolingian palace completed at the turn of the 9th century made Aachen the main royal residence of the Frankish Empire under [[Charlemagne]]. Granted city rights in 1166 by [[Frederick Barbarossa]], it hosted the coronations of German kings from 936 to 1531, until Frankfurt became the preferred site. Home to RWTH Aachen University, a leading technical university, it is known for *Aachener Printen*, a gingerbread.

American singer, actress and model, known as the "Princess of R&B" and credited with helping to redefine contemporary R&B, pop and [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]]. Raised in [[Detroit]], she signed with a record label at 12. Her debut album, *Age Ain't Nothing but a Number* (1994), was largely written and produced by [[R. Kelly]], her mentor. The follow-up, *One in a Million* (1996), made with producers Timbaland and Missy Elliott, sold more than eight million copies worldwide. Her acting debut was in *Romeo Must Die* (2000). She died in a plane crash in the Bahamas, and posthumous releases have continued her commercial success.

[[India|Indian]] actor, filmmaker and television host who works in Hindi films, referred to in the media as "Mr. Perfectionist". He produced *Lagaan* (2001), nominated for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film, and directed *Taare Zameen Par* (2007). His films *3 Idiots* (2009) and *Dangal* (2016) were among the highest-grossing Indian films. He founded Aamir Khan Productions in 1999 and hosted the television talk show *Satyamev Jayate*. The [[Government of India]] awarded him the Padma Shri in 2003 and the Padma Bhushan in 2010.

Medium-sized, burrowing, nocturnal mammal native to [[Africa]]. Its Afrikaans name means earth pig, a reference to its burrowing, although it is not closely related to pigs. It is the only living member of the order Tubulidentata and is an afrotherian, a group that includes elephants, manatees and hyraxes. It is found over much of the southern two-thirds of the continent, avoiding mainly rocky areas, and feeds almost entirely on [[Ant|ants]] and [[Termite|termites]], which it digs out with powerful claws. It digs burrows for shelter and to rear its young. Its closest living relatives are elephant shrews, tenrecs and golden moles. The species is classified as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List.

American lawyer and politician, third vice president of the United States (1801–1805) under [[Thomas Jefferson]]. Burr served in the [[United States Senate]] from 1791 to 1797 and helped form the Jeffersonian Democratic-Republican Party. He was not chosen as Jefferson's running mate in 1804, and that year he killed [[Alexander Hamilton]] in a [[Duel|duel]]. In 1807 he was arrested in [[Alabama]] on charges of treason over an alleged plot to create an independent country, and he was acquitted at each trial. He later resumed practicing law in [[New York City]].

American composer, conductor and teacher known as the "Dean of American Music". Born in [[Brooklyn]], he studied in Paris, working for three years with [[Nadia Boulanger]]. In the 1930s and 1940s he wrote in a deliberately accessible "vernacular" style, producing the ballets *Appalachian Spring*, *Billy the Kid* and *Rodeo*, *Fanfare for the Common Man* and his Third Symphony. His open, slowly changing harmonies evoke the American landscape and are often regarded as characteristic of American music. From the late 1940s he adopted twelve-tone techniques, as in his Piano Quartet (1950), but unlike [[Arnold Schoenberg]] he used tone rows as sources for melodies and harmonies rather than as complete statements. From the 1960s he concentrated increasingly on conducting, and he recorded much of his music for [[Columbia Records]].

American screenwriter, playwright and filmmaker, born in [[New York City]] and known for fast-paced dialogue and "walk and talk" scenes. He created the television series *Sports Night* and *The West Wing*, and his Broadway play *A Few Good Men* (1989) was adapted into the 1992 film. His screenplay for *The Social Network* (2010) won the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay. Other film screenplays include *Moneyball* (2011) and *Steve Jobs* (2015), and he made his directorial debut with *Molly's Game* (2017).

Hand-operated calculating device in which beads slide on rods or in grooves within a frame. Also called a counting frame, it was used from ancient times in the Near East, Europe, China and Russia, and it supports addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and square and cube roots. Each rod usually represents one digit in a base-ten positional system. The Sumerian abacus appeared between 2700 and 2300 BC. It was widely used in Europe as late as the 17th century but fell out of use with the spread of decimal notation and written methods. It was largely replaced by handheld [[Calculator|electronic calculators]] during the 1980s, although merchants in parts of Eastern Europe, Russia, China and Africa still use it. It is also used to teach arithmetic to children in Japan and China.

Sea snails of the genus *Haliotis*, the only genus in the family Haliotidae. The flattened, ear-shaped shell has a row of respiratory holes and an iridescent nacre interior. The largest species, *Haliotis rufescens*, reaches 300 mm (12 in). The flesh is widely considered a delicacy and is eaten raw or cooked in many [[Cuisine|cuisines]]. Abalone graze on [[Kelp|kelp]] and other algae, and [[Aquaculture|aquaculture]] has expanded to supply the market. Intense commercial fishing has depleted many wild stocks, and several species are endangered.

Iranian film director, screenwriter, poet and photographer, a figure of the Iranian New Wave. Born in [[Tehran]], he worked as a painter, graphic designer and advertiser before making films. His first film, *The Bread and Alley* (1970), was a short. His documentary-style narratives often featured child protagonists, rural villages and conversations filmed from stationary cameras inside cars, and they frequently blended fiction and documentary. The *Koker* trilogy (1987–1994), *Close-Up* (1990) and *The Wind Will Carry Us* (1999) won critical acclaim. *Taste of Cherry* (1997) received the Palme d'Or at the [[Cannes Film Festival]]. In a 2018 poll by [[BBC]] Culture, *Where Is the Friend's House?* (1987) and *Close-Up* ranked among the 100 best foreign films.

Shah of Safavid Iran (r. 1588–1629), generally considered the most important ruler of the [[Safavid dynasty]]. He came to the throne at 16 after a coup, then took control of the state. To reduce the power of the Qizilbash tribal army, he built a force of slave-soldiers of Circassian, Georgian and Armenian origin and a regular army that reported directly to him. He fought the Ottoman Empire and the Uzbeks, regaining the South Caucasus and Dagestan. He moved the capital to [[Isfahan]], transforming it into a masterpiece of Safavid architecture, and he sought economic and diplomatic ties with Western countries. In his later years he had several of his sons killed or blinded.

Third Islamic caliphate, ruled from Iraq by the Abbasid dynasty, with [[Baghdad]] as its capital for most of its history. The dynasty descended from Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, an uncle of Muhammad, and came to power in 750, when the Abbasid Revolution overthrew the [[Umayyad Caliphate]]. The second caliph, al-Mansur, founded Baghdad in 762, and the reign of [[Harun al-Rashid]] (r. 786–809) marked the height of Abbasid power. Baghdad became a center of science and culture, home to the [[House of Wisdom]]. From the 9th century provinces grew autonomous, and by the 10th century the caliphs were figureheads while the Buyids and Seljuk Turks held real power. The caliphate effectively ended in 1258, when the [[Mongols]] sacked Baghdad. A surviving branch of the dynasty was reinstated in Cairo by the [[Mamluk]] sultans in 1261, but it had no political power.

Eleventh studio album by [[The Beatles]], released by Apple Records in 1969. It was the last album the group recorded, although *Let It Be* was released later. It topped the charts in the United States and the United Kingdom and has sold over 30 million copies. Side two contains a long medley of songs, and the album includes two George Harrison songs, "Something" and "Here Comes the Sun", considered among his best. The cover, showing the band crossing the zebra crossing outside Abbey Road Studios, is among the most imitated in music history.

American comedy duo of Bud Abbott and Lou Costello, the most popular comedy team of the 1940s and 1950s. They met in 1935 at a [[Burlesque|burlesque]] theater in New York City, with Abbott as the straight man and Costello as the dimwitted comic. Their patter routine "Who's on First?" was first performed for a national radio audience in 1938 and is among the most famous comedy routines of all time. Their films included *One Night in the Tropics* (1940), *Buck Privates* (1941) and *Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein* (1948). They were among the highest-paid entertainers in the world during the [[World War II|Second World War]].

Founder of the Isma'ili [[Fatimid Caliphate]], the only major Shi'a caliphate in Islamic history, and eleventh Imam of the Isma'ili branch of Shi'ism. Born Sa'id ibn al-Husayn, he led the secret Isma'ili missionary network and in 899 claimed the imamate for himself, causing a schism whose followers became the Qarmatians. Bedouin uprisings in Syria in 902–903 forced him to flee to Egypt and then to Sijilmasa in present-day Morocco. In 909 his missionary Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i, leading the [[Berbers|Kutama Berbers]], overthrew the Aghlabid dynasty of Ifriqiya, and he was proclaimed caliph in January 910. In 921 he moved his court to the newly built palace city of Mahdiya on the [[Tunisia|Tunisian]] coast. Two invasions of Egypt failed, and his war with the Byzantine Empire produced raids but no lasting gains. He was succeeded by his son al-Qa'im.

Fifth Umayyad caliph (r. 685–705), who reunited the caliphate after a civil war. After defeating the rival caliph Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who held [[Mecca]], he killed him in 692. Umayyad armies advanced into [[Anatolia]], and Carthage was destroyed and Kairouan recaptured in 698, paving the way for the conquest of western North Africa and the [[Iberian Peninsula]]. He made Arabic the language of administration, introduced a single Islamic currency, and centralized provincial government in Damascus. He also built the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, the earliest archaeologically attested religious monument built by a Muslim ruler.

Emir of Córdoba (r. 912–929) and first caliph of Córdoba (r. 929–961). He took the title al-Nasir li-Din Allah, meaning Defender of God's Faith, after supporting the [[Berbers|Maghrawa Berbers]] against Fatimid expansion in North Africa. In 929 he elevated the emirate to a caliphate. He crushed internal rebellions and built the palace-city of Medina Azahara. Northern Christian kingdoms fought him at Valdejunquera and Simancas, but by the end of his reign they paid him homage. His reign of about half a century was known for religious tolerance.

Founder and first emir of the Emirate of Córdoba (r. 756–788). A member of the Umayyad dynasty from [[Damascus]], he escaped the Abbasid overthrow of the Umayyads in 750 by fleeing through [[Palestine (region)|Palestine]] and North Africa to [[Al-Andalus|al-Andalus]]. In 756 he proclaimed himself emir there and defeated the Fihrid governor Yusuf al-Fihri. His government in Iberia broke with the Abbasids. He built a professional army loyal to the emir rather than to tribal factions and began the Great Mosque of Córdoba. The dynasty he founded lasted nearly three centuries. He was known by the surnames al-Dakhil, meaning the Immigrant, and Saqr Quraysh, meaning the Falcon of Quraysh.

Egyptian military officer and politician, president of Egypt since 2014. As defense minister he led the armed forces in removing President Mohamed Morsi in July 2013. Security forces then dispersed pro-Morsi sit-ins in [[Cairo]], killing an estimated 800 to more than 1,000 people, which Human Rights Watch described as crimes against humanity. Sisi was elected in 2014 and re-elected in 2018 and 2023, when other candidates were barred or boycotted. Critics describe his government as authoritarian; supporters credit it with stability and with projects such as the 2015 expansion of the [[Suez Canal]].
